mainTopic: Sages caught up in husbands' vows against their wives, and the start of the chapter נערה המאורסה
overview: This amud finishes a long series of stories about vows and commands between husbands and wives. First, a ברייתא tells how רבי ישמעאל paid for a gold tooth for a girl, and how he was eulogized as the one who 'clothed' the daughters of Israel. Next, a man vows that his wife cannot benefit from him until רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון taste her cooking. רבי יהודה tastes, learning a קל וחומר from the סוטה waters that one should give up honor for peace. רבי שמעון refuses, to protect the honor of Torah scholars and so people won't get used to vowing. In another case, a wife spits on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's clothes, and רבינא rules that this is a great humiliation, so it fulfills the vow. רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי frees a wife from her husband's vow by finding that her name, לכלוכית, is 'יפה' (fitting). A Babylonian man's wife misunderstands his words and breaks lamps on בבא בן בוטא's head, and he blesses her for doing her husband's will. The chapter רבי אליעזר then ends, and the new chapter נערה המאורסה opens: a betrothed girl's father and husband together cancel her vows.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל gives the girl a gold tooth
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא adds that the girl had a false tooth, and רבי ישמעאל paid for a gold tooth for her.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: She had a false tooth, and רבי ישמעאל made her a gold tooth with his own money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds one more detail to the story it just told, about how רבי ישמעאל made a girl beautiful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story just before this, a man refused to marry a girl because he thought she was ugly. This ברייתא tells us one way רבי ישמעאל fixed that: he replaced her ugly false tooth with a gold one, and he paid for it himself.

phrases.english: It was taught: She had a false tooth,
phrases.notes: 'She' is the girl from the story just before this, whom רבי ישמעאל made beautiful so the man would marry her.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yishmael made for her
a tooth of gold from his own money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a detail to the רבי ישמעאל story from the previous section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל personally paid to make the girl beautiful by giving her a gold tooth.

steps.title: The eulogy for רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: When רבי ישמעאל died, a eulogizer called on the daughters of Israel to cry for the man who dressed them up.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי ישמעאל died, a certain eulogizer began like this: 'Daughters of Israel, weep for רבי ישמעאל, who clothed you,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רבי ישמעאל was eulogized, praising him for beautifying the Jewish girls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eulogizer borrows the words of דוד's lament over שאול and applies them to רבי ישמעאל. 'Who clothed you' means he made the girls beautiful, so they could get married, like the girl with the gold tooth.

keyTerms.meaning: Who clothed you (who made you beautiful)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל was so devoted to helping girls get married that he was remembered as the one who 'clothed the daughters of Israel.'

phrases.english: When Rabbi Yishmael died,
a certain eulogizer opened about him like this:
"Daughters of Israel, weep for Rabbi Yishmael,
phrases.notes: This copies דוד's words about שאול: שמואל ב 1:24.

phrases.english: who clothed you, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי שְׁכֵיב רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ הַהוּא סַפְדָנָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the רבי ישמעאל story by describing how he was remembered.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל was eulogized as the one who beautified the daughters of Israel.

steps.title: A husband's vow tied to two rabbis tasting his wife's cooking
steps.stepSummary: A man vows that his wife may not benefit from him until she has רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון taste her cooking.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his wife: 'It is קונם for you to benefit from me until you have רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון taste your cooking.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new story about a vow. This step only describes the case; the next two steps show how each rabbi reacted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband made his wife's permission to benefit from him depend on two great rabbis tasting her food. That puts the rabbis in a tough spot: tasting saves the marriage, but it lets a husband use them in his fight with his wife.

keyTerms.meaning: His wife (literally, the one of his house)
A word used to make a vow that forbids something, like a קרבן

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his wife:
"Konam that you may not benefit from me
until you give your cooked dish to taste
to Rabbi Yehuda and to Rabbi Shimon."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about a husband's vow and how rabbis responded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife's permission to benefit from her husband depends on two rabbis tasting her food.

steps.title: רבי יהודה tastes to make peace
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה tastes the food, reasoning with a קל וחומר from the סוטה waters that he should give up his honor for שלום בית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה tasted. He said: It is a קל וחומר. If, to make peace between a man and his wife, the תורה said that My Name, written in holiness, should be erased in the cursing waters, even when it is unsure, then all the more so should I give up my honor.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה agrees to taste the food, and he explains why using a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the סוטה ceremony, ה׳'s holy Name is erased in water, just for the chance of making peace in a marriage. If ה׳ gives up His honor for peace, even when it might not work, then a person must certainly give up his own honor for peace.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument from a lighter case to a stronger one

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic source for the huge value of שלום בית: even כבוד שמים is set aside for it.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה טְעֵים, אֲמַר, קַל וָחוֹמֶר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda tasted. He said: It is a kal vachomer:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה לַעֲשׂוֹת שָׁלוֹם בֵּין אִישׁ לְאִשְׁתּוֹ
phrases.english: If, in order to make peace between a man and his wife,
the Torah said: My Name, which was written in holiness,
shall be erased in the cursing waters, even when it is uncertain,
phrases.notes: This is the water a סוטה drinks: במדבר 5:23. It's 'uncertain' because we don't know if she sinned or if peace will come.

phrases.english: then I, all the more so.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה טְעֵים, אֲמַר, קַל וָחוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יהודה's response to the vow described in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should give up his own honor to make peace between husband and wife, learned by קל וחומר from the סוטה.

steps.title: רבי שמעון refuses to taste
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון refuses to taste, to protect the honor of Torah scholars and so people won't get used to making vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון did not taste. He said: Let all the widow's children die, and שמעון will not move from his place. And also: so that people will not get used to making vows.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון takes the opposite approach and refuses to taste, giving two reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His first reason is strong language: even if the family falls apart, he won't let Torah scholars be used as tools in a husband's vow. His second reason is practical: if rabbis always go along, people will keep making vows like this.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה gave up his honor for שלום בית; רבי שמעון refused, to protect the honor of Torah scholars and to stop people from getting used to vowing.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון does not want the family to suffer. 'Let the widow's children die' is a strong way of saying he will not give in to this kind of vow, whatever happens.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon did not taste. He said:
Let all the children of the widow die,
phrases.notes: He means the husband's family: even if the husband dies and leaves a widow and orphans.

phrases.english: and Shimon will not budge from his place.

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹד: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִתְרַגְּלִי לְמִינְדָּר.
phrases.english: And furthermore: so that they will not get used to making vows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite reaction to רבי יהודה's in the same story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Torah scholar should not give up his honor to fulfill such a vow, both for the honor of Torah and so people won't get used to vowing.

steps.title: A vow that the wife must spit on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: A man vows his wife can't benefit from him until she spits on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and she spits on his clothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his wife: 'It is קונם for you to benefit from me until you spit on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.' She came and spat on his clothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells another story of a harsh vow, and how the wife tried to fulfill it by spitting on the rabbi's clothes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow said to spit 'on' רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, but she spat only on his clothing, not on his body. This sets up the question in the next step: did she really fulfill the vow?

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his wife:
"Konam that you may not benefit from me

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁתָּרוֹקִּי בּוֹ בְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל״.
phrases.english: until you spit on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel."
She came and spat on his clothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא דְּאָמַר לִדְבֵיתְהוּ ״קֻוֽנָּם שֶׁאִי אַתְּ נֶהֱנֵית לִי עַד שֶׁתָּרוֹקִּי בּוֹ בְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story of a husband's vow that involves a rabbi's honor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife tried to fulfill the vow by spitting on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's clothing.

steps.title: Did spitting on his clothes really fulfill the vow?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי asks רבינא how spitting on the clothes counts, since the husband wanted to humiliate the rabbi himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: But this man meant to humiliate him!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדפתי challenges whether the wife really fulfilled the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's goal was to shame רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. Spitting on clothes seems like less than spitting on the person, so maybe the husband's intent was not met and the vow is still in force.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
But this man intended humiliation!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the action in the previous step fulfilled the vow.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that spitting on his clothing fulfilled the vow.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The husband wanted to humiliate the rabbi; spitting on clothes seems not to achieve that, so the vow should not be fulfilled.

steps.title: Spitting on his clothes is a great humiliation
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that spitting on the clothes of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is itself a great humiliation, so the vow is fulfilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Spitting on the clothes of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is a great humiliation.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge and says the wife did fulfill the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a man as great as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, spitting even on his clothes is a big insult. So the husband's intent to humiliate was met, and she may benefit from him again, while she avoided spitting on the rabbi's body.
steps.whatToRemember: Spitting on a great rabbi's clothes counts as humiliating him, so it fulfilled the vow without spitting on him directly.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: מִירָק עַל מָנֵי דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
phrases.english: Spitting on the clothes of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
is a great humiliation.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִירָק עַל מָנֵי דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל זִילוּתָא רַבְּתָא הִיא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what counts as humiliation for so great a person.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only spitting on the rabbi himself would humiliate him and fulfill the vow.
steps.terutzMaskana: Spitting on the clothes of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is already a great humiliation, so the vow is fulfilled.

steps.title: A husband vows until his wife shows something beautiful to רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: A man forbids his wife from benefiting from him with a קונם until she shows something beautiful about herself to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who told his wife: 'It is קונם for you to benefit from me until you show רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי something beautiful about you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a husband's vow that depends on a sage. This line sets up the case, and the next steps show how the sage deals with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow is a קונם, which forbids the wife from getting any benefit from her husband. It lasts until one condition is met: she must show the sage a beautiful feature. The husband seems to think there is nothing beautiful about her, so the vow looks impossible to undo.

keyTerms.meaning: Usually means a blemish; here it means any feature of her body

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his wife:
"It is konam that you may not benefit from me
until you show some beautiful feature that is in you
phrases.notes: Literally 'a beautiful מום'. Here it doesn't mean a blemish, just any part of her that's nice.

phrases.english: to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another story in the same series as step 6: a husband's vow against his wife that involves a sage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife is forbidden to benefit from her husband until she shows a beautiful feature of hers to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל checks her features one by one
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי asks about each of her features, hoping to find one that is beautiful, but each answer is negative.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked: Maybe her head is beautiful? They said: It's round. Maybe her hair? It looks like flax stalks. Her eyes? Narrow. Her ears? Double-sized. Her nose? Stubby. Her lips? Thick. Her neck? Short. Her stomach? Swollen. Her feet? Wide like a goose's. Maybe her name is beautiful? Her name is לכלוכית.
steps.whatsHappening: The sage is searching for anything beautiful about the woman so he can free her from the vow. This step builds up to the punchline in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sage wants to help the couple, so he tries feature after feature from head to feet. Every answer fails, which shows how hard the condition was. When he finally asks about her name, the answer seems like one more failure, but it gives him the opening he needs.

phrases.english: He said to them: Perhaps her head is beautiful?
They said to him: It is round.
Perhaps her hair is beautiful?
It looks like stalks of flax.
Perhaps her eyes are beautiful? They are narrow.
Perhaps her ears are beautiful? They are double in size.
Perhaps her nose is beautiful? It is stubby.
Perhaps her lips are beautiful? They are thick.
Perhaps her neck is beautiful? It is low and short.
Perhaps her stomach is beautiful? It is swollen.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא רַגְלֶיהָ נָאוֹת? רְחָבוֹת כְּשֶׁל אֲווֹזָא.
phrases.english: Perhaps her feet are beautiful? They are wide like a goose's.
Perhaps her name is beautiful? Her name is "Likhlukhit."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The sage starts trying to meet the condition from step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is there any feature of this woman that can be called beautiful?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Every physical feature is described as unattractive, and her name is לכלוכית.

steps.title: Her name fits her, so he permits her
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי says her name לכלוכית is 'fitting' because she is 'soiled' with blemishes, and he permits her to her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is fitting that they call her לכלוכית, since she is soiled with blemishes. And he permitted her.
steps.whatsHappening: The sage finds his loophole: her name is 'יפה', meaning 'fitting'. So the vow is fulfilled and he permits her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יפה means both 'beautiful' and 'fitting.' The husband said she must show something יפה, and her name is יפה in the sense that it fits her perfectly. That counts as fulfilling the condition, so she may benefit from her husband again.

keyTerms.meaning: Beautiful, and also fitting or proper
Her name; it sounds like 'dirty one'

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the sage is insulting her for fun. He is using the double meaning of יפה ('beautiful' and 'fitting') to satisfy the vow's condition and free her.
steps.whatToRemember: A sage can fulfill a vow's condition through a clever but true reading of its words. Here יפה means 'fitting', and her name fit her.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: יָפֶה קוֹרִין אוֹתָהּ לִכְלוּכִית
phrases.english: He said to them: It is fitting that they call her Likhlukhit,
phrases.notes: יָפֶה is the same word the husband used. Here it means 'fitting' instead of 'beautiful', and that's the trick.

phrases.english: since she is soiled with blemishes,
and he permitted her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: יָפֶה קוֹרִין אוֹתָהּ לִכְלוּכִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the search from step 10 by finding that her name is 'יפה' (fitting).
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Her name is יפה in the sense of fitting, so the vow's condition is fulfilled and she is permitted to her husband.

steps.title: A Babylonian husband and the dialect mix-ups
steps.stepSummary: A Babylonian man marries a woman in ארץ ישראל. She keeps taking his words literally or in her own dialect: two lentils, a whole סאה, and lamps instead of gourds.
steps.simpleTranslation: A Babylonian man went up to ארץ ישראל and married a woman. He told her: Cook me two lentils. She cooked exactly two lentils, and he got angry. The next day he said: Cook me a סאה. She cooked a whole סאה. He said: Go bring me two בוצינא. She went and brought him two lamps.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about a wife who does exactly what her husband says, even when she misunderstands him. This step sets up the dramatic ending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each time, the husband uses a loose expression or a Babylonian word, and she takes it literally or in the meaning used in ארץ ישראל. 'Two lentils' meant 'a few', and 'a סאה' meant 'a lot'. בוצינא meant 'gourds' to him but 'lamps' to her.

keyTerms.meaning: Gourds in Babylonian Aramaic; lamps in the Aramaic of ארץ ישראל

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא בַּר בָּבֶל דִּסְלֵיק לְאַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: There was a certain Babylonian who went up to Eretz Yisrael
and married a woman.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: בַּשִּׁילִי לִי תְּרֵי טַלְפֵי.
phrases.english: He said to her: Cook me two lentils.
phrases.notes: He meant 'a few lentils', a normal way of talking.

phrases.english: She cooked him two lentils.
He got angry at her.

phrases.aramaic: לִמְחַר אֲמַר לַהּ: בַּשִּׁילִי לִי גְּרִיוָא.
phrases.english: The next day he said to her: Cook me a se'ah.
phrases.notes: This time he meant 'a big amount' so she wouldn't make too little again.

phrases.english: She cooked him a whole se'ah.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: זִילִי אַיְיתִי לִי תְּרֵי בוּצִינֵי.
phrases.english: He said to her: Go bring me two butzinei.
phrases.notes: In his Babylonian dialect בוצינא means a small gourd. In ארץ ישראל it meant a lamp.

phrases.english: She went and brought him two lamps.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא בַּר בָּבֶל דִּסְלֵיק לְאַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story, connected to the theme of a wife carrying out her husband's words even when a sage is involved.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife carries out every instruction exactly, according to her literal or local understanding of his words.

steps.title: She breaks the lamps on בבא בן בוטא's head
steps.stepSummary: The angry husband tells her to break the lamps on the 'head of the בבא' (gate). She breaks them on the head of the sage בבא בן בוטא, who was judging at the gate.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: Go break them on the head of the בבא. בבא בן בוטא was sitting at the gate judging a case. She went and broke them on his head.
steps.whatsHappening: The misunderstandings reach their peak: the wife breaks the lamps on a great sage's head. This step sets up the sage's surprising reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Babylonian Aramaic בבא means 'gate', so the husband meant the top of the gate. She didn't know that word, but a sage named בבא was sitting right there. So she obeyed by breaking them on his head.

keyTerms.meaning: Gate in Babylonian Aramaic; also the name of the sage בבא בן בוטא

phrases.english: He said to her: Go break them
on the head of the bava.
phrases.notes: He meant the top of the gate. She heard בבא as a person's name.

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה יָתֵיב בָּבָא בֶּן בּוּטָא אַבָּבָא
phrases.english: Bava ben Buta was sitting at the gate
and judging a case.
She went and broke them on his head.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לַהּ: זִילִי תְּבַרִי יָתְהוֹן עַל רֵישָׁא דְבָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 12 with the final and most dramatic misunderstanding.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Following her husband's words as she understood them, the wife breaks the lamps on the sage בבא בן בוטא's head.

steps.title: בבא בן בוטא blesses her for obeying her husband
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא asks what she did. She says her husband told her to, and he blesses her with two sons like him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: What is this you did? She said: This is what my husband told me. He said: You did your husband's will. May God give you two sons like בבא בן בוטא.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the sage not getting angry at all. He blesses the woman because she was trying to do what her husband wanted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of focusing on his own hurt and embarrassment, בבא בן בוטא focuses on her good intention: doing what her husband wanted. Like רבי יהודה in step 4, he sets aside his own honor. The 'two sons' match the two lamps she broke.
steps.whatToRemember: בבא בן בוטא did not get angry at the woman who broke lamps on his head. He blessed her for trying to do her husband's will.
steps.whyThisMatters: It echoes the approach of רבי יהודה in step 4, who set aside his own honor for the sake of a married couple, as opposed to רבי שמעון in step 5.

phrases.english: He said to her: What is this that you did?
She said to him: This is what my husband commanded me.
He said: You did your husband's will,
may the Omnipresent bring forth from you
two sons like Bava ben Buta.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story from steps 12 and 13 with the sage's reaction.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A wife who sincerely does her husband's will deserves blessing, and a sage gives up his own honor to honor that.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא formally closes the chapter called רבי אליעזר with the traditional הדרן line.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter called רבי אליעזר. It is not a new argument; it is a closing formula said when a chapter is finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chapter is named after its first words, רבי אליעזר. Saying הדרן עלך expresses a promise to come back and learn this chapter again. Everything after this line belongs to a new chapter.

keyTerms.meaning: "We will return to you": the line said at the end of every chapter
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא

steps.whatToRemember: The story of בבא בן בוטא and the other stories were the last part of the chapter רבי אליעזר. A new topic starts right after this line.

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter Rabbi Eliezer

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter right after the final story about בבא בן בוטא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter רבי אליעזר is complete.

steps.title: New chapter: father and husband cancel a betrothed girl's vows
steps.stepSummary: The opening משנה of the new chapter נערה המאורסה rules that a betrothed young woman's father and husband are the ones who cancel her vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: A betrothed young woman: her father and her husband cancel her vows.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter begins with a new משנה. It tells us who has the power to cancel the vows of a נערה המאורסה: both her father and her husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נערה is a young girl who is still under her father's authority. Once she is מאורסה (has had אירוסין, the first stage of marriage), she is partly connected to her husband too. So this משנה names both her father and her husband as the ones who are מפירין her נדרים.

keyTerms.meaning: A young girl in the stage right after she becomes an adult, still under her father's authority
Betrothed: she has had אירוסין but has not yet moved in with her husband

steps.whyThisMatters: This opening rule sets the topic for the whole new chapter: how the father and the husband share the power of הפרת נדרים for a betrothed girl.

phrases.english: A betrothed young woman,
her father and her husband cancel her vows.

steps.triggerLanguage: נַעֲרָה הַמְאוֹרָסָה, אָבִיהָ וּבַעְלָהּ מְפִירִין נְדָרֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a brand-new chapter and topic after the הדרן closing line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a נערה המאורסה, her father and her husband are the ones who cancel her vows.
